topic: the 1518 dancing plague in Strasbourg -- why hundreds of people danced themselves to exhaustion and death
title: The 1518 'Plague' That Made 400 People Dance Until Some Died
description: AI-narrated commentary. In 1518, hundreds of people in Strasbourg danced uncontrollably for weeks -- some until they died. It wasn't poison. Historians now think it was a real stress response, triggered by years of famine and fear.

hook_candidates.text: In 1518, hundreds of people caught the 'Dancing Plague' in one German city -- and it wasn't a disease or poison at all.
In July 1518, one woman started dancing in a Strasbourg street -- and by the end of the month, 400 people couldn't stop.
Why did 400 people in one city dance nonstop for weeks in 1518, some of them until they died?
On July 14, 1518, a woman named Frau Troffea stepped into a Strasbourg street and began to dance -- and by week's end, thirty more had joined her.

payoff_mechanism: The dancing wasn't caused by poison or infection at all -- three straight years of famine, disease, and religious fear left people so psychologically overwhelmed that their bodies expressed that trauma as involuntary, uncontrollable movement, a real stress response historians now call mass psychogenic illness.

sources.note: Confirms Frau Troffea's July 1518 outbreak grew to ~400 dancers within a month, with daily deaths from exhaustion.

beats.text: In **1518**, hundreds of people caught the 'Dancing Plague' in one German city -- and it wasn't a disease or poison at all.
It started with one woman, Frau Troffea, dancing alone in a Strasbourg street -- within a week, **thirty** more had joined her.
Doctors at the time -- and for centuries after -- blamed poisoned rye bread, a fungus called **ergot** that causes convulsions.

But ergot can't explain hundreds of people dancing for weeks straight -- historians now say three years of **famine**, disease, and religious fear pushed people into a genuine stress reaction their own bodies expressed as uncontrollable dancing.

Some dancers collapsed from **exhaustion** before it finally stopped -- so next time something's called a plague, remember: sometimes the real cause is the mind, not the body. Follow for more history like this, and let me know what you'd have believed back then.
